Draft_Claim: In real-world card-fraud detection systems, most transactions are not inspected by human investigators and their true labels arrive only after customer dispute or chargeback verification latency, while only top-k alerted transactions receive rapid investigator feedback.
Source_Citation: Dal Pozzolo et al. (2015, IJCNN; 2018, IEEE TNNLS)
Evidence_Location: Dal Pozzolo et al. (2018), Section I & Section III, pp. 3784-3788
Scope_Caveats: Applies to real-world card issuing/processing FDS streams; public static benchmarks do not expose separate feedback vs chargeback timestamps.

Draft_Claim: In the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection benchmark, the labelled training set contains 590,540 transactions across train_transaction and train_identity joined on TransactionID, where identity records exist for only a subset of transactions and TransactionDT is a relative timedelta starting at 86,400 rather than a calendar timestamp.
Evidence_Location: Kaggle Data Description page; Hayat & Magnier (2025), Section 3
Scope_Caveats: While community analyses infer seconds (86,400 = 24*60*60), the calendar anchor is undisclosed and final isFraud labels lack arrival timestamps.
Final_Use: Keep with explicit time-unit and label-provenance caveats

Draft_Claim: Gradient-boosted decision trees augmented with simple neighborhood feature aggregations can match or outperform specialized Graph Neural Networks across multiple supervised graph anomaly detection benchmarks.
Source_Citation: Tang et al. (2023, NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks Track - GADBench)
Scope_Caveats: Demonstrated across 10 static GAD datasets in GADBench; setting-dependent and must be tested under causal temporal protocols rather than assumed universal.
Final_Use: Keep (Motivates B1/B2 strong tree baselines and RQ1/RQ3)

Draft_Claim: Empirical analysis of posterior credit-card fraud detection reports that compromised-card blocking delays follow a skewed latency profile in which roughly 1% of compromised cards are blocked within 1 hour and approximately 30% within 1 day, with the remainder extending over subsequent days and weeks.
Source_Citation: Nguyen et al. (2022, AISTATS / PMLR Vol. 151, pp. 10067-10077)
Scope_Caveats: Measures compromised-card blocking time in an industrial processor dataset, not a universal per-transaction chargeback arrival ground truth for IEEE-CIS.
Verification_Status: Verified 2026-10-24 via PMLR v151 full text
Final_Use: Keep with qualification (Motivates D2 profile-inspired delay scenario)

Draft_Claim: On the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset, a seed-matched comparison between transductive and strictly inductive evaluation protocols reported a 39.5-point F1 gap attributable to training-time exposure to test-period adjacency, with Random Forest outperforming evaluated GNNs under strict inductive visibility.
Scope_Caveats: Single-author preprint on Bitcoin transaction graphs (Elliptic), not payment-card data; cited strictly as a recent methodological lead on topology leakage.
Final_Use: Keep with explicit preprint and domain qualifiers

Draft_Claim: Under Bayes' rule, if genuine transactions do not generate fraud reports in the simulation, fraudulent transactions remain unreported at age a with survival probability S(a) = P(D > a | Y=1), and the pre-report cohort fraud prior is pi, then the posterior probability that an unreported transaction of age a is fraudulent is q(a) = [pi * S(a)] / [pi * S(a) + (1 - pi)].
Source_Citation: Analytical derivation in this study (Step 5 / Section 9.2 of Execution Plan)
Evidence_Location: Section 6 / Section 7 of Manuscript & Protocol v1
Scope_Caveats: Exact under stated conditional independence and zero false-report assumptions; reaches 0 at maturity horizon M if and only if S(M) = 0.
Verification_Status: Verified analytically and via numerical calibration test (test_reproducible_delay_draws.py)
Final_Use: Keep (Core methodological formulation for V2 soft-target loss)

Draft_Claim: A static entity node (such as a card proxy, address, or email domain) connected to all historical and future transactions in a bipartite or multi-relational graph creates a two-hop message-passing path through which future transaction features or labels can leak backward into earlier transaction scores unless edges and entity states are causally constrained to t_j <= t_i.
Source_Citation: Protocol derivation & unit test verification in this study; supported by Khaleghpour & McKinney (2026) and Van Belle et al. (2023)
Evidence_Location: Section 8.2 of Execution Plan; verified by tests/test_no_future_edges.py
Scope_Caveats: Applies to all multi-hop relational aggregators and GNNs on shared-entity transaction graphs.
Verification_Status: Verified 2026-10-24 via automated unit test suite
